title: Analytics: Revenue over 24 Months
description: Sales data from November 2024 to October 2026 with 24 customers, 15 products, 241 orders and 498 order lines. Some values are missing in Segment, Channel and discount, and a few customers have never ordered.

exercises.title: Hardware by price
exercises.description: Show the name and list price of all products in the Hardware category, most expensive first.
hints: Filter by category and sort by price.
ORDER BY ListPrice DESC
SELECT Name, ListPrice FROM Product WHERE Category = 'Hardware' ORDER BY ListPrice DESC

exercises.title: Customer countries
exercises.description: Which countries appear in the customer table? Show each country exactly once, sorted alphabetically.
hints: Without anything extra, each country would appear once per customer.
DISTINCT removes duplicate rows.
SELECT DISTINCT Country FROM Customer ORDER BY Country

exercises.title: Customers without a segment
exercises.description: Which customers don't have a segment yet? Show name and country, sorted by name.
hints: A missing segment is NULL.
Use IS NULL.
WHERE Segment IS NULL ORDER BY Name

exercises.title: Open and shipped orders
exercises.description: Show the id, order date and status of all orders that are not yet completed (status Open or Shipped). Sort by order date and id.
hints: It is enough if one of two values matches.
IN checks several values in a short form.
WHERE Status IN ('Open', 'Shipped')

exercises.title: Orders without a sales channel
exercises.description: How many orders have no sales channel (Channel)? Name the column WithoutChannel.
hints: You need to count NULL values.
Count with COUNT(*) and filter on Channel in WHERE.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS WithoutChannel FROM Orders WHERE Channel IS NULL

exercises.title: Customers without orders
exercises.description: Which customers have never placed an order? Show name, country and sign-up date, sorted by name.
hints: Customers without orders disappear with an INNER JOIN.
LEFT JOIN from Customer to Orders, then check for the missing partner.
WHERE o.Id IS NULL

exercises.title: Order lines with product and customer
exercises.description: For all order lines of the orders with ids 1 to 5, show the customer name, the product name and the quantity. Sort by order id and product name.
hints: You need Orders, Customer, OrderLine and Product.
Start from Orders and join the three other tables.
WHERE o.Id BETWEEN 1 AND 5

exercises.title: Orders per channel
exercises.description: Count the orders per sales channel. Orders without a channel should appear as Unknown. Sort by count, descending (columns Channel and OrderCount).
hints: NULL forms its own group when grouping.
COALESCE(Channel, 'Unknown') replaces NULL. Group by the same expression.
GROUP BY COALESCE(Channel, 'Unknown')

exercises.title: Revenue per product category
exercises.description: Calculate the revenue per product category (Revenue, rounded to 2 decimal places). The revenue of an order line is Quantity * UnitPrice * (1 - discount percent / 100). A missing discount (NULL) means 0 percent. Cancelled orders don't count. Sort by revenue, descending.
hints: The discount can be NULL. Use COALESCE, otherwise the whole row becomes NULL.
Join OrderLine to Orders (for the status) and to Product (for the category).
SUM(l.Quantity * l.UnitPrice * (1 - COALESCE(l.DiscountPercent, 0) / 100.0)) with GROUP BY p.Category

exercises.title: Revenue per month
exercises.description: Calculate the revenue per month (Month as text in the format YYYY-MM, Revenue rounded to 2 decimal places, excluding cancelled orders), sorted chronologically.
hints: The month is the first 7 characters of the date.
SUBSTRING(o.OrderDate, 1, 7) gives the format YYYY-MM. Group by it.
GROUP BY SUBSTRING(o.OrderDate, 1, 7) and ORDER BY Month

exercises.title: High-revenue customers
exercises.description: Show customers (Name) with a total revenue above 10000 (Revenue, rounded, excluding cancelled orders), highest revenue first.
hints: Calculate the revenue per customer first, then filter the groups.
The condition on SUM belongs in HAVING.
HAVING SUM(l.Quantity * l.UnitPrice * (1 - COALESCE(l.DiscountPercent, 0) / 100.0)) > 10000

exercises.title: Products sold with a high discount
exercises.description: Show all products (Name) that were sold on at least one order line with a discount of more than 10 percent, sorted alphabetically.
hints: Find the ProductIds of the order lines with a discount above 10.
IN with a subquery on OrderLine.
WHERE Id IN (SELECT ProductId FROM OrderLine WHERE DiscountPercent > 10)

exercises.title: Orders above average
exercises.description: Show the ids of the orders whose revenue (Revenue, excluding cancelled) is above the average revenue of all non-cancelled orders. Sort by id.
hints: First calculate the revenue per order in a derived table.
The average over these revenues is a second subquery.
WHERE Revenue > (SELECT AVG(Revenue) FROM (...) x)

exercises.title: First order per customer
exercises.description: For each customer with orders, find the first order (order id and date). If the date is the same, the smaller id wins. Sort by customer id.
hints: Number each customer's orders and keep number 1.
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerId ORDER BY OrderDate, Id) in a derived table, then WHERE rn = 1 on the outside.
Window functions can't be used directly in WHERE. Put them in a subquery.

exercises.title: Cumulative monthly revenue
exercises.description: For each month, show the revenue and the running total since the start (Running, rounded to 2 decimal places). Use the monthly revenues excluding cancelled orders, sorted chronologically.
hints: First calculate the monthly revenue as a derived table.
SUM(Revenue) OVER (ORDER BY Month) adds up continuously.
ROUND(SUM(Revenue) OVER (ORDER BY Month), 2) AS Running

exercises.title: Change from the previous month
exercises.description: For each month, show the revenue, the revenue of the previous month (Previous) and the change (Change, rounded to 2 decimal places). For the first month, both are NULL. Sorted chronologically.
hints: You need the value of the previous row.
LAG(Revenue) OVER (ORDER BY Month) returns the previous month, NULL in the first month.
ROUND(Revenue - LAG(Revenue) OVER (ORDER BY Month), 2) AS Change

exercises.title: Moving three-month average
exercises.description: For each month, calculate the average revenue of the current and the two previous months (Avg3, rounded to 2 decimal places). At the start, fewer months are available. Sorted chronologically.
hints: You need a window frame of three rows.
AVG(...) OVER (ORDER BY ... ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
ROUND(AVG(m.Revenue) OVER (ORDER BY m.Month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS Avg3

exercises.title: Customer rank per country
exercises.description: Assign a rank within each country by total revenue (CountryRank, highest revenue = 1). Show country, name, revenue and rank. Sort by country and rank.
hints: The rank should start again at 1 in every country.
RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY Country ORDER BY Revenue DESC)
First calculate the revenue per customer in a derived table.

exercises.title: Share of total revenue
exercises.description: For each customer with revenue, show the share of total revenue in percent (SharePercent, rounded to one decimal place). Sort by share, descending, then by name.
hints: You need the sum over all customers in every row.
SUM(Revenue) OVER () is a sum over the whole result.
ROUND(Revenue * 100.0 / SUM(Revenue) OVER (), 1) AS SharePercent

guidedScenarios.title: Window functions: comparing months
guidedScenarios.description: You build a view with monthly revenues and apply window functions to it: rankings, running totals, comparison with the previous month and moving averages. The scenario creates a view and resets the database at the start.

steps.title: Create monthly revenues as a view

queryExplanation.summary: A view (VIEW) stores a query under a name. The following steps use MonthlyRevenue like a table.

parts.explanation: Creates the view. It stores no data itself, but runs the underlying query each time it is accessed.
Cuts the first 7 characters out of the date YYYY-MM-DD, which is the month.
Counts orders, not order lines. One order has several lines.
Revenue of an order line including the discount. If the discount is missing (NULL), 0 percent applies.
Cancelled orders don't count.

steps.resultExplanation: The query returns no rows. The view has been created.
steps.databaseEffect: New view MonthlyRevenue with the columns Month, OrderCount and Revenue. No data is copied.

steps.title: Look at the monthly revenues

queryExplanation.summary: The view returns one row per month. The following steps build on it.

parts.explanation: The view is queried like a table.
Chronological, because YYYY-MM sorts correctly as text.

steps.resultExplanation: 24 rows from 2024-11 to 2026-10. Revenue fluctuates strongly: in August 2025 it was only 980.50, in March 2026 it was 19,756.38.

steps.title: Rankings and ties

queryExplanation.summary: Window functions calculate a value for every row without collapsing rows. Three ranking functions differ in how they handle ties.

parts.explanation: The window: all rows, sorted by order count in descending order.
Consecutive number without gaps and without ties. With the same count, the month decides here.
A tie gets the same rank, followed by a gap.
A tie gets the same rank, and numbering continues without a gap.

steps.resultExplanation: October 2026 (15 orders) and September 2026 (14) are in the lead. After that, November 2025, March 2026 and May 2026 have 12 orders each: RANK gives rank 3 three times and then jumps to 6, DENSE_RANK gives 3 three times and then 4. ROW_NUMBER numbers them 3, 4 and 5 instead.
steps.databaseEffect: Nothing, the query only reads. The window functions only add columns to the result.

steps.title: Running total

queryExplanation.summary: SUM as a window function adds up all rows from the start to the current row. This produces a cumulative value.

parts.explanation: Sum of all months up to and including the current row.
Rounds to avoid floating-point residue from the addition.

steps.resultExplanation: The last row (2026-10) shows 223,002.75: the total revenue of the 24 months. At the turn of the year 2025/2026, the total stood at 107,693.25.

steps.title: Comparison with the previous month

queryExplanation.summary: LAG reads the value of an earlier row. The first month has no predecessor, so LAG returns NULL there.

parts.explanation: The revenue of the row before, in chronological order.
Change from the previous month. NULL minus a number stays NULL.

steps.resultExplanation: The first row (2024-11) has NULL in PreviousRevenue and Change. The largest increase was May 2025 (+13,203.88), the largest decrease June 2025 (-14,364.23).

steps.title: Moving average

queryExplanation.summary: A window frame (ROWS BETWEEN) limits which rows go into the calculation. Here it is the current row and the two previous rows.

parts.fragment: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
parts.explanation: Frame of at most three rows: two before and the current one.
Average over the frame only, hence a moving average.

steps.resultExplanation: The curve is smoother than the monthly values. The first two rows average only 1 and 2 months (9,698.88 and 7,952.37), after that always three. The last value (2026-10) is 13,505.22.

guidedScenarios.title: Window functions: comparing customers by group
guidedScenarios.description: With PARTITION BY you split the window into groups. You determine a customer's rank within their country, the best customer per country, the share of total revenue and each customer's first order. At the end you see why 3 customers are missing. The scenario creates a view and resets the database at the start.

steps.title: Create customer revenues as a view

queryExplanation.summary: The view summarizes the revenue per customer. It contains only customers with at least one non-cancelled order, because the INNER JOIN filters out the others.

parts.explanation: Creates the view.

parts.fragment: INNER JOIN Orders ... INNER JOIN OrderLine
parts.explanation: Joins each customer with their orders and order lines.
One row per customer.

steps.resultExplanation: The query returns no rows. The view has been created.
steps.databaseEffect: New view CustomerRevenue with the columns CustomerId, Name, Country and Revenue.

steps.title: Rank overall and per country

queryExplanation.summary: PARTITION BY splits the rows into groups. The window function is calculated separately for each group, so the rank starts again at 1 in every country.

parts.explanation: Rank across all customers.

parts.fragment: RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY Country ORDER BY Revenue DESC)
parts.explanation: Rank within the country only.

steps.resultExplanation: 21 rows. Rheinwerk Systems GmbH is at rank 1 overall with 25,839.03 and also at rank 1 in Deutschland. Brouwer Techniek BV is at rank 2 overall and at rank 1 in the Niederlande. Pierre Martin is at rank 21 overall and at rank 4 in Frankreich.

steps.title: The best customer per country

queryExplanation.summary: Window functions can't be used in WHERE. So you calculate the number in a subquery and filter on it on the outside.

parts.fragment: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Country ORDER BY Revenue DESC)
parts.explanation: Numbers the customers of each country by revenue.
Derived table: the subquery behaves like a table with the alias t.
Keeps only the first customer of each country.

steps.resultExplanation: 5 rows, one per country: Lukas Brandner (Österreich), Atelier Rivage SAS (Frankreich), Rheinwerk Systems GmbH (Deutschland), Brouwer Techniek BV (Niederlande) and Alpen Outdoor AG (Schweiz).

steps.title: Share of total revenue

queryExplanation.summary: OVER () with nothing inside means the window is the entire result. This makes the grand total available in every row.

parts.explanation: Total revenue of all customers, repeated in every row.
Share in percent. The 100.0 with a decimal point prevents integer division.
Shows only the five largest shares.

steps.resultExplanation: Rheinwerk Systems GmbH accounts for 11.6 percent of revenue, Brouwer Techniek BV for 8.7 and Atelier Rivage SAS for 8.2. The five largest customers together reach about 42 percent.

steps.title: Each customer's first order

queryExplanation.summary: The same pattern returns the first row per group, here the oldest order of each customer.

parts.fragment: PARTITION BY o.CustomerId ORDER BY o.OrderDate, o.Id
parts.explanation: Number chronologically per customer. The id resolves ties in the date.
Only the first order.

steps.resultExplanation: 21 rows for 21 customers. Customer 1 has their first order (no. 19) on 2024-12-28, customer 5 (no. 1) on 2024-11-04. Customers 12, 23 and 24 don't appear because they have never ordered.

steps.title: Why are 3 customers missing?

queryExplanation.summary: Window functions only see the rows the join leaves over. To find customers without orders, you need a LEFT JOIN and a check for NULL.

parts.explanation: Keeps all customers, even those without orders.
Only customers without orders.
Replaces a missing segment with a text.

steps.resultExplanation: 3 customers have never ordered: Helga Moser and Lena Hofmann (both without a segment, hence unbekannt) and Katharina Auer (segment Consumer). They are the reason why the view contains 21 instead of 24 customers.
